title: US Military Strikes Iranian Missile Sites While Deal Talks Continue; Trump: 'Proceeding Nicely'; Rubio Says Deal Language Could Take 'Couple of Days'
detail: May 26, 2026 — Even as US-Iran nuclear deal negotiations continued, US military forces conducted 'self-defense strikes' targeting Iranian missile launch sites and boats in and around the Strait of Hormuz. The Pentagon characterized the strikes as necessary defensive action against proximate Iranian military activity, maintaining a distinction between the tactical military track and the diplomatic track. Trump told reporters that the overall deal talks were 'proceeding nicely,' and Secretary of State Rubio stated publicly that deal language finalization could 'take a couple of days' — suggesting the framework text remains in active drafting rather than a completed document ready for signing. Iran's IRGC reported that 25 commercial vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz within a 24-hour period under Iranian oversight, framing the strait as already operationally open under their supervision — Iran's long-standing position in negotiations. The Quad foreign ministers (US, Australia, India, Japan) meeting in New Delhi discussed Hormuz threats to global shipping as a multilateral concern, with India particularly focused on the energy supply chain impact. The White House addressed the apparent contradiction of simultaneous strikes and deal-making by framing the military action as defensive and distinct from the diplomatic track. Oil markets continued pricing in a near-term deal despite the fresh strikes, with traders assessing the military activity as tactical rather than a breakdown in the broader framework. The 14-point MOU remains the public baseline: Phase 1 would require Hormuz to reopen within 30 days with Iran permitted to freely sell oil; Phase 2 would be a 60-day window for nuclear negotiations and sanctions relief sequencing.

title: Colombia Election 5 Days Away: CNC Poll Shows Near-Technical Tie (Cepeda 33.4% vs De la Espriella 30.9%); Peace Architecture at Stake as ELN Ceasefire Holds
detail: With Colombia's May 31 first-round presidential election five days away, the latest CNC poll (conducted May 16-22) shows the race in a near-tie between Iván Cepeda (Historic Pact/left, 33.4%) and Abelardo De la Espriella (far-right, 30.9%) — within the margin of error. This contrasts sharply with the Invamer poll showing Cepeda leading at 44.6% vs. De la Espriella at 31.6%, and Guarumo at 37.1% vs. 27.5%. The sharp divergence between polling houses creates genuine uncertainty about who will qualify for the June 21 runoff. De la Espriella has surged approximately 10.5 percentage points since early May, a historically unusual late-campaign movement. The ELN's unilateral pre-election ceasefire remained nominally in force as of May 26, offering a degree of security calm in the final days. The peace-architecture stakes crystallize the election's national significance: a Cepeda presidency would resume ELN talks suspended since the January 2025 Catatumbo massacre, continue the JEP, and potentially re-engage FARC-EMC dissidents; a De la Espriella presidency would immediately terminate all peace negotiations; a Valencia presidency would pivot to military-first counterinsurgency while maintaining the JEP. Foreign Policy's May 22 analysis highlighted election-related violence risks from armed groups as a key concern in the final week. The Americas Quarterly noted that the conservative vote is effectively split between De la Espriella and Valencia, with neither positioned to take second place without the other's collapse.
